claims.text: A 2–3 nm high-entropy oxide overlayer can be deposited by ALD on the nearly equiatomic automotive alloy catalyst.
A post-deposition defect or porosity-control step can produce controlled porosity in the oxide overlayer.
ALD at approximately 150–200 °C using precursors corresponding to the principal alloy elements will form the intended overlayer.
The deposited high-entropy oxide will form a continuous, conformal nanoscale film on the alloy substrate.
Engineered porosity in the film will preserve reactant access to catalytic active sites.
The oxide overlayer will act as a protective barrier between the alloy catalyst and aggressive exhaust species.
The protective overlayer will inhibit thermal sintering of the catalyst.
Controlled overlayer porosity will permit sufficient reactant diffusion to the underlying active sites.
High configurational entropy of the oxide will enhance its stability during thermal cycling and prolonged operation.
The untreated catalyst progressively loses activity during transient low-temperature exhaust operation.
Sintering and corrosion by reactive exhaust components cause the untreated catalyst's durability limitations.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the ALD-treated catalyst will exhibit less activity decay over simulated mileage.
The ALD-treated catalyst will have improved resistance to thermal aging.
The ALD-treated catalyst will have improved resistance to degradation caused by H2O and NO.
The overlayer will sustain catalytic performance without increasing platinum-group-metal consumption.
The proposed benefit is expected during transient operation at 300–500 °C in gas streams containing H2O and NO and under thermal-aging protocols.
